messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marcus

Marcus was forty-three years old when his F-16 went down. He had been a combat pilot for two decades, had flown over Iraq and Afghanistan, had seen colleagues killed in action—experiences that had hardened him but had not broken him. What broke him was an equipment failure over the Nevada desert during a routine training run. The hydraulic system ruptured without warning. He felt the stick go dead in his hands, felt the aircraft yaw violently, felt the g-forces slam him sideways as the nose pitched down. There was a moment—perhaps two seconds, though it felt like an eternity—when he knew the ejection system might not work, when the ground was rushing up and the roar of the dying engines filled his skull. The ejection fired. He rocketed free. His parachute deployed. But those seconds had rewritten something fundamental in how his brain understood safety and control.

The accident investigation found no pilot error. Marcus had done everything right. He had survived. Yet in the thirteen years since, he had come to believe with unshakeable certainty that the world was fundamentally dangerous in ways he could not predict or prevent, that his body was a fragile machine liable to betray him at any moment, and that the only way forward was through absolute vigilance and control. He felt dead inside—not depressed in the classical sense, but hollowed out, as if the part of him that had once found joy in flying, in his marriage, in the simple pleasure of a meal shared with friends, had been incinerated in that cockpit. His wife, Catherine, had watched him become someone else: a man who flinched at unexpected sounds, who sat with his back to the wall at restaurants, who seemed to be listening always for something catastrophic just beyond the horizon.

When a low-frequency boom echoed across the neighborhood—a sonic boom from the air base, the kind of sound that had once been ordinary to him—Marcus's body seized. His muscles locked, his heart hammered, his breath came in shallow gasps. The sound of an explosion, even a distant one, sent him into a state of high alert that lasted for hours. These moments of sensory threat triggered an immediate cascade of avoidance. He stopped attending air shows with Catherine, stopped going to restaurants near the highway where truck backfires might startle him, stopped accepting invitations to social gatherings where he could not control the acoustic environment. The more he avoided these situations, the more his body remained in a state of constant tension, muscles coiled, reflexes hair-trigger. When Catherine suggested they visit her sister in California, Marcus felt a wave of dread—the flight itself, the airports, the possibility of turbulence or mechanical noise—and he declined. He had declined so many invitations over the years that Catherine had largely stopped asking.

His physical health had become another arena of control and dread. A few years after the crash, he had experienced chest pain—nothing serious, the cardiologist said—but the experience had terrified him. Now the sight of an ambulance, the smell of a hospital, the thought of a routine physical examination triggered the same cascade of panic and avoidance. He had not had a complete physical in eight years. Instead, he had developed an elaborate system of dietary restriction, eating only foods he deemed "safe," counting calories obsessively, convinced that by controlling his intake and his weight he could prevent illness, could maintain the bodily integrity that felt constantly under siege. When Catherine suggested he see a doctor about his weight loss, he became angry, defensive—her concern felt like an accusation, a reminder that his body was failing him. The restriction gave him a sense of agency in a world that had proven itself fundamentally uncontrollable.

Each avoidance, each act of control, each restriction seemed to confirm his darkest beliefs. The world remained dangerous. His body remained vulnerable. He remained vigilant, hyperalert, scanning for threats that never fully materialized yet always felt imminent. When he starved himself or avoided crowds or turned away from Catherine's touch, the temporary relief he felt—the illusion of control—only deepened his conviction that the world required this constant, exhausting defense. His marriage had become a kind of parallel life: Catherine in one room, Marcus in another, both of them trapped in a pattern neither could break. At fifty-six, he had come to his first therapy appointment not because he believed change was possible, but because Catherine had finally issued an ultimatum, and because some part of him—the part that still remembered the man he had been—recognized that he could not live this way much longer.
